query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing modest Al doping into FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings promotes formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer at high temperatures, thereby reducing surface friction and limiting subsurface plastic strain during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on steel substrate with minimal Al content (<1 at%)
generation.intervention: Incrementally increase the Al content (e.g., 2–5 at%) in the FeNiCrCoCu coating composition
generation.conditions: High-temperature pin-on-disk wear testing in air at 600–800 °C, under comparable contact stresses and sliding speeds
generation.structural_mediator: Stable Al-rich oxide scale acting as a barrier against direct metal-metal contact and plastic shear
generation.mechanism: Al additions facilitate preferential formation of protective oxide layers that reduce oxidation-driven wear and suppress plastic flow at asperities by limiting frictional heat buildup
generation.predicted_outcome: Al-doped coatings exhibit measurably lower wear loss and diminished evidence of local plastic deformation compared to the undoped baseline under the same conditions
generation.baseline: Wear and deformation measurements from the undoped or minimally Al-doped FeNiCrCoCu coating tested identically
generation.boundary: For Al doping levels up to ~5 at% and testing temperatures up to ~800 °C under moderate normal loads; higher Al content or higher temperatures may introduce alternative phases or embrittlement phenomena
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in wear or deformation remain to be experimentally established, and microstructural heterogeneity may affect oxide scale formation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare baseline (minimal Al) and Al-doped FeNiCrCoCu coatings, perform pin-on-disk tests at 600–800 °C in air. Characterize wear rates, friction coefficients, and cross-sectional oxide morphologies via microscopy and compositional analysis.
measurements: mass loss or volume loss from the coating
cross-sectional microstructure (via TEM/EDS) indicating oxide layer evolution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Al-doped coatings do not exhibit a thicker or more stable oxide scale, and show equal or worse wear loss and plastic deformation compared to the baseline, then the stated hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
